title: Contract extension: Senior transportation services (Transdev)
summary:
This item would extend the county's contract with Transdev Services, Inc. of Lombard, Illinois, for 12 more months, for up to $9.59 million, to provide transportation for Senior Services and Behavioral Health programs. Terms would stay the same, and the extension runs January 1, 2027, through December 31, 2027. title: Requiring a full Board vote on voting delegates to county associations
summary:
Vice Chair Abdur-Rahman's resolution would require that anyone chosen to cast Fulton County's votes at the National Association of Counties (NACo) and the Association County Commissioners of Georgia (ACCG) be approved by a vote of the full Board of Commissioners. No single commissioner, including the Chair, could name a voting delegate without the Board's prior approval. If this conflicts with NACo or ACCG rules, those rules would control only to the extent of the conflict.

Approved October 21, 2026, 5–0, with 1 not voting. Results from the October 21, 2026 meeting come from the clerk’s draft record, which the board is scheduled to ratify on November 4, 2026.
whyItMayMatter: The choice of who casts Fulton County's votes in state and national county associations would be made by the full Board rather than by the Chair alone.

title: Directing development of policies on generative AI use in county government
summary:
Commissioner Barrett's resolution would direct the County Manager, Chief Information Officer and County Attorney to develop a plan for a county policy on the use of generative artificial intelligence (AI), including disclosure rules, tools and training. The plan would be due by the first meeting in December 2026 so costs could be considered for the 2027 budget. Until a fuller policy exists, commissioners' resolutions and ordinances would need County Attorney review and would first appear as "First Reads" before a vote at a later meeting.

Removed from the October 21, 2026 agenda. It had not come back for a vote as of the board’s October 21, 2026 meeting. The same request also appears as item 26-0679 (October 7, 2026). Results from the October 21, 2026 meeting come from the clerk’s draft record, which the board is scheduled to ratify on November 4, 2026.
whyItMayMatter: Commissioners' proposed resolutions and ordinances would be presented at one meeting and voted on at a later one, allowing more review before votes.

title: Urging limits on corporate and private equity ownership of medical practices
summary:
Commissioner Barrett's resolution would state the Board's support for the federal "Stop Corporate Takeovers of Physicians Act of 2026" and urge Congress to pass it. It would also urge the Georgia General Assembly to pass similar protections for physician ownership and control of medical practices, with more transparency about who owns them. The resolution cites the county's proposed 2027 health care premiums, which show an 11.47 percent cost increase and list private equity ownership as one reason. Copies would go to Georgia's congressional delegation and state leaders.

The motion to approve failed on October 21, 2026 (3 yes, 0 no, 2 absent, 1 not voting). The same request also appears as item 26-0678 (October 7, 2026). Results from the October 21, 2026 meeting come from the clerk’s draft record, which the board is scheduled to ratify on November 4, 2026.
whyItMayMatter: The resolution would not change any law itself; it asks Congress and the Georgia General Assembly to limit corporate control of medical practices.

title: Removing the 5% cap on 2027 departmental budget requests
summary:
Commissioner Barrett's resolution would remove the 5% cap the Budget Commission placed on what county departments may request for the 2027 budget, and ban such caps going forward. It would amend county code Sec. 2-261 so the proposed budget must include all budget requests from departments, agencies, elected officials and authorities. Departments could submit 2027 requests left out because of the cap, to be included in the proposed budget presented on November 15, 2026.

The motion to approve failed on October 21, 2026 (1 yes, 1 no, 2 absent, 2 not voting). Results from the October 21, 2026 meeting come from the clerk’s draft record, which the board is scheduled to ratify on November 4, 2026.
whyItMayMatter: People reviewing the proposed 2027 county budget would see every department's full funding requests.

title: Including county taxes in Alpharetta's North Point Mall tax allocation district
summary:
Commissioners Ellis and Thorne's resolution would let some Fulton County property taxes count toward the City of Alpharetta's Tax Allocation District number three at North Point Mall and Activity Center, under an agreement with the city. The agreement says the district's main purpose is to secure a National Hockey League team. County consent would end December 31, 2030, if the city has not secured an NHL expansion team and signed arena lease by then, unless the county extends that deadline. The county's total contribution would be capped at $192.42 million.

Approved with changes on October 21, 2026, 6–0. The approved version differs from the original proposal; the item record has the details. Results from the October 21, 2026 meeting come from the clerk’s draft record, which the board is scheduled to ratify on November 4, 2026.
whyItMayMatter: Growth in county property taxes from the North Point area could go toward redevelopment costs, including a hockey arena, for up to 30 years.

title: The future of senior transportation services
summary: After an assessment of the senior transportation program on August 19, 2026, the board directed staff to start talks with MARTA about MARTA paying for, and possibly running, the program, and to report back within 90 days. On October 7, 2026 the board held (postponed) a request to extend the current contract with Transdev Services for all of 2027, for up to $9,589,074.96.
whyItMayMatter: No decision has been made yet on who will provide senior rides in 2027. The program serves older adults and Behavioral Health clients.

title: Encouraging community gardens and food resilience
summary: A resolution encouraging home, school, faith-based and community gardens, food-preservation education, and support for local farmers, in response to fertilizer and food supply problems, failed on September 16, 2026 with 3 votes, short of the 4 needed. It passed on October 7, 2026 with 4 votes.
whyItMayMatter: The resolution encourages action and asks for a public-education effort; it does not fund a program by itself.

title: Limiting public comment at board meetings
summary: A proposed change would have limited spoken public comment at board meetings to topics reasonably related to items on that meeting’s agenda, and set rules for handling disruptions. It was held on September 16, 2026. On October 7, 2026 the motion to approve it failed for lack of a second.
whyItMayMatter: Public comment is how residents speak directly to commissioners at meetings. The current rules stay in place.

title: Ordinance abolishing the Board of Ethics for an independent hearing officer system
summary:
Commissioner Arrington's ordinance would rewrite the county's ethics code, abolish the Fulton County Board of Ethics and have independent hearing officers decide ethics complaints instead. Hearing officers would be Georgia attorneys with at least 10 years of practice, and no current or former Ethics Board member could serve. Complaints would generally have to be filed within two years of the alleged violation, a preliminary review would be due within 60 days, and cases should usually end within one year. Parties could seek review in Fulton County Superior Court.

Removed from the October 7, 2026 agenda at the request of Commissioner Arrington. It had not come back for a vote as of the board’s October 21, 2026 meeting.
whyItMayMatter: People who file ethics complaints involving county officers or employees would have them decided by independent hearing officers on set deadlines instead of by the Board of Ethics.

title: 2026 county property tax rates
summary: On September 16, 2026 the board proposed keeping the General Fund rate at 8.87 mills, which is above the rollback rate, so Georgia law required three public hearings (two on September 30 and one on October 7). On October 7 a motion for the lower rollback rate (8.822 mills, according to the county’s Finance presentation) failed for lack of a second. The board then adopted 8.87 mills for the General Fund, 0.169 mills for the Bond Fund, and 9.431 mills for the Fulton Industrial District, by a vote of 4 yes, with one abstention and one commissioner not voting.
whyItMayMatter: This rate is used to calculate the county share of property tax bills. Because it is above the rollback rate, the county describes it as a tax increase.

title: A rewrite of the county ethics code
summary: The board approved a resolution introducing a revised Code of Ethics. It would abolish the Board of Ethics and have independent officers, who are experienced attorneys, screen and decide ethics complaints. The County Attorney was directed to prepare an ordinance to adopt it. The vote was 4-1, with one commissioner absent. The new code takes effect only once the board adopts that ordinance, which had not come up for a vote as of the board’s October 21, 2026 meeting.
whyItMayMatter: The revised code is not in effect yet; it still needs an adopting ordinance.

title: Abolishing dormant funds and moving balances to the General Fund
summary:
Commissioner Ellis's resolution would immediately abolish seven county funds with little or no recent activity, including the Wolf Creek Fund, the Business Court Fund, Salute to the Arts, the NACO Conference fund and two tree funds, and confirm the earlier closure of the Indigent Defense Committee fund. Remaining money would move to the County General Fund unless the law requires otherwise, and future revenue would go there too. It would repeal the county code section tied to the Tree Plant Trust Fund, with closing steps done by December 31, 2026.

Approved October 7, 2026, 5–0, with 1 absent.
whyItMayMatter: Leftover money in these inactive funds would move into the county's General Fund.

title: Video calls between lawyers and people held in county jails
summary: The board approved up to $108,000 in 2026 for a secure communications system, such as the My Justice Portal platform, that lets lawyers talk confidentially with people held in county detention facilities using tablets already in the jails. Staff were also asked to find up to $327,725 for 2027 in next year’s proposed budget.
whyItMayMatter: Easier contact with lawyers can reduce delays in cases.

title: Resolution on private equity in health care
summary: A resolution would have urged Congress and the Georgia General Assembly to limit corporate and private equity ownership of medical practices, citing rising health care costs. On October 7, 2026 the motion to approve it failed for lack of a second.
whyItMayMatter: The resolution was not adopted.

title: Directing development of policies on generative AI use in county government
summary:
Commissioner Barrett's resolution would direct the County Manager, Chief Information Officer and County Attorney to develop a plan for a county policy on the use of generative artificial intelligence (AI), including disclosure rules, tools and training. The plan would be due by the first meeting in December 2026 so costs could be considered for the 2027 budget. Until a fuller policy exists, commissioners' resolutions and ordinances would need County Attorney review and would first appear as "First Reads" before a vote at a later meeting.

The motion to approve died for lack of a second on October 7, 2026. The same request also appears as item 26-0727 (October 21, 2026).
whyItMayMatter: Commissioners' proposed resolutions and ordinances would be presented at one meeting and voted on at a later one, allowing more review before votes.

title: A county policy on artificial intelligence
summary: The board directed the County Manager to develop policies and procedures for how county government uses artificial intelligence, by a vote of 5-0 with one commissioner absent. A separate, more detailed AI resolution (26-0679) failed for lack of a second at the same meeting.
whyItMayMatter: The policy is still to be written by county staff.

whyItMayMatter: These rates set what county employees and retirees pay for health coverage next year.

title: Funding for the trial calendar, My Justice Portal and forensic lab testing
summary:
Commissioner Ellis's resolution would provide up to $1 million for the rest of fiscal year 2026 for three efforts aimed at people held in Fulton County detention facilities. It would return the Consolidated Trial Calendar, which handles serious violent felony cases, to a monthly schedule; fully set up the My Justice Portal so detained people can talk confidentially with their lawyers; and pay private labs for forensic testing. The County Manager would report quarterly on spending and results, including average length of jail stays.

Removed from the September 16, 2026 agenda. It had not come back for a vote as of the board’s October 21, 2026 meeting.
whyItMayMatter: The resolution says these steps would reduce the average length of stay at Fulton County detention facilities and the backlog of pending criminal cases.

title: Abolishing two court technology funds and moving balances to the General Fund
summary:
Commissioners Ellis and Thorne's resolution would close two court technology funds: Fund 419, which holds e-recording fees, and Fund 439, which holds e-filing fees. Once adopted, those fees would go to the County General Fund instead, and both funds would be abolished December 31, 2026, with remaining balances moved to the General Fund. The fees would not be reduced, and court and land records technology would be funded through the regular budget. Technology purchases using county funds would need review by the Chief Information Officer.

Approved August 19, 2026, 4–1, with 1 absent.
whyItMayMatter: People who pay e-filing and e-recording fees would pay the same amounts, but the money would be budgeted through the county's General Fund.

title: Releasing funds for affordable commercial space for small businesses on the Westside
summary:
Commissioner Barrett's resolution would let the county use $2.5 million of its share of Westside Tax Allocation District (TAD) money for a Strategic Property Acquisition Fund being created by Invest Atlanta. The fund would help buy, fix up and hold underused properties so they can provide affordable space for local small businesses, grocery options and affordable housing. Invest Atlanta is starting these funds with $23 million in total across the Westside, Perry Bolton and Stadium TADs.

Earlier: held on July 15, 2026. Removed from the August 5, 2026 agenda. It had not come back for a vote as of the board’s October 21, 2026 meeting.
whyItMayMatter: Small businesses on Atlanta's Westside could gain access to more stable, affordable commercial space.

title: Dissolving the HIV/AIDS Prevention, Care, and Policy Advisory Committee
summary:
Commissioner Ellis's resolution would dissolve the Fulton County HIV/AIDS Prevention, Care, and Policy Advisory Committee, which it says has not met in more than two years. The committee was created in 2017 to update the Strategy to End AIDS in Fulton County. It would end on September 4, 2026, and all appointments to it would terminate. Its records would go to the Clerk to the Commission and the Fulton County Department for HIV Elimination.

Approved August 5, 2026, 5–0, with 1 not voting.
whyItMayMatter: The resolution says the committee's remaining duties could be handled by the Fulton County Board of Health and the Department for HIV Elimination, with community input still coming through the Metropolitan Atlanta HIV Health Services Planning Council.

title: Rules change: items with four or more no votes are not automatically continued
summary:
Commissioner Ellis's resolution would change the Board's meeting rules so that any voting item getting four or more "no" votes is treated as finally denied. Today, an item that fails to get four "yes" votes is automatically carried over to the next meeting for another vote. Under the change, only items without four votes either way, such as a tie, would still carry over. Commissioners could still bring a new or substantially amended item, or a motion to reconsider.

Approved August 5, 2026, 6–0.
whyItMayMatter: Items rejected by four or more commissioners would no longer automatically return to later meeting agendas.

title: A new Budget Commission

It has four members: the county manager, the chief financial officer, one commissioner from districts 1–3, and one from districts 4–6. whyItMayMatter: The commission shapes the budget that decides how county money is spent each year.

whyItMayMatter: A resolution states the board’s position; it does not by itself stop a development authority from acting.

whyItMayMatter: Voters, not the board, make the final decision on November 3, 2026. The tax would add to the sales tax paid on purchases in the area where it applies.

title: Grant for a 149-unit affordable multifamily development in downtown Atlanta
summary:
Commissioners Barrett and Abdur-Rahman's resolution would let the county use $750,000 of its share of Westside Tax Allocation District (TAD) money to help build Folio House, a 149-unit apartment building by Gorman & Company, LLC at 143 Alabama Street SW in Downtown Atlanta. All units would stay affordable for 30 years for households earning 30%, 50% or 80% of the area median income. It is the second phase of redeveloping the 1947 former Atlanta Constitution building, which has been vacant for decades.

Approved July 15, 2026, 6–0.
whyItMayMatter: Lower-income households could gain access to 149 Downtown Atlanta apartments that would stay affordable for 30 years.

title: Grant to restore historic downtown Atlanta storefronts and support small businesses
summary:
Commissioners Barrett and Abdur-Rahman's resolution would let the county use $50,000 of its share of Westside Tax Allocation District (TAD) money as a grant to the Atlanta Preservation Center, Inc. The money would help restore historic storefront facades at the Muses Lofts, 50-70 Peachtree Street NE in Downtown Atlanta, covering seven storefronts between Walton Street and Poplar Street. The total project budget is $557,200. Two vacant storefronts, including the former site of Alonzo Herndon's Crystal Palace barber shop, would get extra restoration.

Approved July 15, 2026, 5–0, with 1 not voting.
whyItMayMatter: Seven storefronts on Peachtree Street, including ones used by local small businesses, would get restored facades, and vacant units would be prepared for tenants.

title: Grant to support 194 new jobs and a Mercedes-Benz investment
summary:
Commissioners Barrett and Abdur-Rahman's resolution would let the county use $125,000 of its share of Westside Tax Allocation District (TAD) money as a grant to Mercedes-Benz Research and Development North America, Inc. The company would redevelop existing buildings at 384 Northyards Blvd. on the Westside into a 60,530-square-foot research and development facility expected to create 194 new jobs. Mercedes-Benz would invest $32.9 million, and the county's share is part of a $500,000 Westside TAD grant within a $4 million incentive package.

Approved July 15, 2026, 6–0.
whyItMayMatter: The facility is expected to bring 194 new jobs to Fulton County and give area students and graduates paths into high-growth careers.

title: Opposing extension of City of Atlanta Tax Allocation Districts; participation policy
summary:
Commissioners Ellis and Abdur-Rahman's resolution formally opposes the City of Atlanta's plan, approved by the Atlanta City Council on June 15, 2026, to extend six of its eight tax allocation districts (TADs) for 30 more years through 2056, and declines the county's consent. It sets conditions for any future county TAD participation, including a reset of tax baselines, a cap on the county's contribution and audit rights, and requires at least five commissioners to approve. It directs county staff to pursue legal remedies if needed.

Approved July 15, 2026, 4–1, with 1 abstaining.
whyItMayMatter: The resolution says extending the districts without resetting tax baselines could cost Fulton County up to $85 million a year in property tax revenue.

title: Grant to restore the historic George Towns and Grace Towns Hamilton Homes
summary:
This resolution would let part of Fulton County's share of Westside Tax Allocation District (TAD) money be granted to the Atlanta Development Authority to help restore and preserve the George Towns and Grace Towns Hamilton homes at 582 and 594 University Place in Vine City. Invest Atlanta and Preserve Black Atlanta, Inc. are partnering on the $2.3 million project, which also uses a $1 million National Park Service historic preservation grant. Grace Towns Hamilton was the first African American woman elected to the Georgia General Assembly.

Approved June 17, 2026, 5–0, with 1 not voting.
whyItMayMatter: Two deteriorated historic homes tied to Atlanta's Civil Rights history would be restored, which the resolution says would remove blight without displacing residents.

title: Grant for a 20-unit affordable multifamily development in English Avenue

Brawley Boulevard NW in the English Avenue neighborhood. Sixteen of the 20 units would be affordable for 30 years for households at 60%, 70% and 80% of area median income. The developer, Clifford Palmer, is a long-time English Avenue resident.

Approved June 17, 2026, 5–0, with 1 not voting.
whyItMayMatter: Lower-income households would gain 16 new affordable apartments built on vacant property in English Avenue, without displacing existing residents.

title: Site preparation grant for the Andrew Young international institute in Vine City
summary:
This resolution would let $500,000 of Fulton County's share of Westside Tax Allocation District (TAD) money be granted to the Andrew J. Young Foundation for site preparation for the Andrew Young International Institute for Peace and Reconciliation in Vine City. The institute is a planned 80,000-square-foot cultural and educational center next to Rodney Cook Sr. Park, with a total budget of $100 million. This site preparation phase costs $2,510,765, and the foundation has a 100-year, $1-a-year ground lease from the City of Atlanta.

Approved June 17, 2026, 5–0, with 1 not voting.
whyItMayMatter: Vine City would see site work begin for a planned institute that the resolution says will offer free public hours, event space and educational programs.

title: Correcting a scrivener's error in the 0.75 percent transportation sales tax resolution
summary:
This resolution by Commissioners Ellis and Thorne would fix a clerical error in Resolution 21-0535 (August 2, 2021), which set up the 0.75% transportation special purpose local option sales tax (TSPLOST) in Fulton County outside the City of Atlanta. The earlier resolution set the tax's maximum net proceeds at $545,954,720 instead of the correct $627,847,927. Voters approved the tax on November 2, 2021, and it runs five years, from April 1, 2022 to March 31, 2027.

Approved June 3, 2026, 5–0, with 1 absent.
whyItMayMatter: The correction sets the most the voter-approved transportation sales tax can raise for transportation projects at about $627.8 million instead of $546 million.

title: Policy on keeping commissioners' personal staff after a Board vacancy
summary:
Chairman Pitts's resolution would change the Board's policy on what happens to a commissioner's personal staff when the commissioner dies, is removed or resigns. Under the 2019 policy, staff could stay on for a transition period of no more than 90 days. The change would let retained staff of the vacated district stay employed as needed to keep serving that district until the seat is filled, with the Chairman acting as their appointing authority.

Approved June 3, 2026, 4–0, with 1 absent and 1 not voting.
whyItMayMatter: Residents of a commission district whose seat becomes vacant could keep getting help from the district's staff until a new commissioner takes office.

title: Redirecting unspent Superior Court funds to the Magistrate Court
summary:
Chairman Pitts's resolution would move money in the 2026 budget from the Superior Court to the Magistrate Court. In 2023 the Board shifted $780,000 a year from Magistrate Court to Superior Court to pay for three full-time magistrates who help with Superior Court's criminal caseload. Under an agreement between the two courts, those magistrates will now be paid from Magistrate Court's budget, so the unspent part of the $780,000 for 2026 would be returned to it.

Approved May 20, 2026, 5–0, with 1 not voting.

title: Asking the Sheriff to decline certain misdemeanor bookings to ease jail overcrowding
summary:
Chairman Pitts's resolution would ask, but not require, the Fulton County Sheriff to use existing authority under Georgia law to decline jail bookings for certain non-violent misdemeanors, such as criminal trespass, marijuana possession, urban camping and public drunkenness, where appropriate and consistent with public safety. The resolution cites jail overcrowding and the expected rise in visitors and enforcement during the 2026 FIFA World Cup. The Sheriff controls jail intake and booking.

Approved May 20, 2026, 5–0, with 1 not voting.
whyItMayMatter: People arrested for some low-level, non-violent misdemeanors might not be booked into the jail if the Sheriff chooses to follow the Board's request.

title: Challenging the constitutionality of House Bill 369 on nonpartisan county elections
summary:
This resolution, sponsored by Commissioners Arrington, Abdur-Rahman and Barrett, opposes Georgia House Bill 369 and challenges its constitutionality. HB 369, signed May 12, 2026, requires nonpartisan elections for certain county officers and district attorneys in Clayton, Cobb, DeKalb, Fulton and Gwinnett counties beginning in 2028. The resolution urges the General Assembly to reconsider, directs the County Attorney to recommend legal options to fight the law, and sends copies to Georgia's legislators and Congressional delegation.

Approved May 20, 2026, 4–0, with 2 not voting.
whyItMayMatter: The resolution itself does not change HB 369; it states the Board's opposition and asks the County Attorney for possible legal challenges to how Fulton voters elect some county offices and the district attorney.

title: Setting minimum annual funding for Quality Living Services and Sadie G. Mays
summary:
Commissioner Arrington's resolution would set a minimum annual funding level of $250,000 for Quality Living Services, Inc. and Sadie G. Mays Health and Rehabilitation Center, subject to money being set aside in the county's yearly budget. Quality Living Services supports seniors with housing, social services and cultural programs, and Sadie G. Mays is a nursing facility offering skilled nursing and rehabilitation. The County Manager and Finance Department would recommend a funding source, and the Board would review the amount each year.

Earlier: held on April 15, 2026. The motion to approve failed on May 6, 2026 (2 yes, 0 no, 2 abstaining, 2 not voting).
whyItMayMatter: Seniors and nursing-care patients served by these two organizations would have a set minimum level of county support each year, subject to the annual budget.

title: Directing the County Manager to find funding for the Summer Youth Internship Program
summary:
Commissioner Arrington's resolution would direct the County Manager, working with the Finance Department, to find $500,000 in the county budget to continue Fulton County's Summer Youth Internship Program. The County Manager would bring funding recommendations back to the Board for review and approval. A staff presentation says the 2026 program would serve youth ages 16 to 24 at no less than $15 an hour, and that $500,000 would serve about 333 youth.

Earlier: held on April 15, 2026. The motion to approve failed on May 6, 2026 (2 yes, 0 no, 2 abstaining, 2 not voting).
whyItMayMatter: Fulton County youth ages 16 to 24 could have paid summer work opportunities; the staff presentation says no funding for the program was allocated in the 2026 General Fund budget.

whyItMayMatter: County senior service centers and the North Point Parkway facility could receive donated tables, chairs, desks and other furniture.

title: Grant for a 26-unit affordable multifamily development in English Avenue

All units would be affordable for 30 years for households at 30%, 60% and 80% of area median income. The money is already held by Invest Atlanta and, per the resolution, does not affect the county's 2026 budget.

Approved with changes on May 6, 2026, 6–0. The approved version differs from the original proposal; the item record has the details.
whyItMayMatter: Lower-income households would gain 26 new affordable apartments on a vacant lot in English Avenue, without displacing existing residents.

title: Grant for 14 permanently affordable homes for sale in English Avenue
summary:
This resolution would let $350,000 of Fulton County's share of Westside Tax Allocation District (TAD) money be granted to Atlanta Land Trust, Inc. and Westside Future Fund to build 14 permanently affordable duplex and single-family homes for sale in the English Avenue neighborhood. The homes would use a community land trust model, which keeps them affordable long term while letting families build equity. The money is already held by Invest Atlanta and, per the resolution, does not affect the county's 2026 budget.

Approved with changes on May 6, 2026, 6–0. The approved version differs from the original proposal; the item record has the details.
whyItMayMatter: Income-eligible families could buy one of 14 new permanently affordable homes built on vacant lots in English Avenue.

title: Promoting public education on how to obtain voter identification
summary:
Commissioner Thorne's resolution would require public-facing Fulton County facilities, as determined by Voter Education and Outreach, to display a standard notice explaining how residents can get valid voter identification. The notice would include a QR code linking to current voter ID information on the county website. The County Manager would make sure the notices are created and kept up to date, and the resolution says it does not advocate for or against any party, candidate or ballot measure.

whyItMayMatter: Visitors to county facilities would see posted guidance on getting voter ID; the resolution notes voters without an accepted ID can get a free voter ID card from Registration and Elections or the Department of Driver Services.

title: Grant for North & Oliver Apartments affordable housing in English Avenue
summary:
This resolution would let $1 million of Fulton County's share of Westside Tax Allocation District (TAD) money be granted to North & Oliver Apartments, LLC to help build a 120-unit apartment building in the English Avenue neighborhood. All units would be affordable for 30 years, with 96 of them at 60% of area median income or below. The money is already held by Invest Atlanta and, per the resolution, does not affect the county's 2026 budget.

Approved April 15, 2026, 6–0.
whyItMayMatter: Lower-income households would gain 120 new affordable apartments at 851 North Avenue NW, built on a vacant lot without displacing existing residents.

title: Up to twelve workweeks of paid parental leave for county employees
summary:
Chairman Pitts's resolution would amend Personnel Procedure 205-16 so that eligible Fulton County employees can take up to 12 workweeks of paid parental leave, up from the current 8 workweeks. Paid parental leave covers the birth, adoption or placement of a child. Human Resources would update the policy, and the County Manager and Finance Department would identify any funding or budget changes needed.

Approved with changes on April 15, 2026, 5–0, with 1 not voting. The approved version differs from the original proposal; the item record has the details.
whyItMayMatter: Eligible county employees who have, adopt or take placement of a child could receive up to four more weeks of paid leave.

title: Funding Atlanta Volunteer Lawyers Foundation services for intimate partner abuse survivors
summary:
Vice Chair Abdur-Rahman's resolution would give $975,000 to the Atlanta Volunteer Lawyers Foundation to support its services for survivors of intimate partner abuse and their families. The nonprofit runs the Safe Families Office in the Fulton County Courthouse, which the resolution says helps over 3,000 survivors a year and has lost federal funding. A revised version says the money would come, to the extent possible, from the county's opioid settlement funds rather than tax revenue.

Earlier: held on March 18, 2026. Approved April 1, 2026, 6–0.
whyItMayMatter: Survivors of intimate partner abuse seeking legal help at the Fulton County Courthouse would have the Safe Families Office's services supported with county funds.

title: Locality pay for Superior Court judges of the Atlanta Judicial Circuit
summary:
Commissioner Ellis's resolution would authorize locality pay of up to $20,106 a year for Superior Court judges of the Atlanta Judicial Circuit who join the new state judicial pay plan, in place of the existing county salary supplement. The locality pay would automatically drop if the state raises judges' salaries. Judges would keep their county fringe and retirement benefits, the Chief Judge's supplement would continue, and judges who do not join the new plan would keep their current supplement.

Approved April 1, 2026, 6–0.
whyItMayMatter: Superior Court judges in the new state pay plan would receive county locality pay of up to $20,106 a year instead of the current county supplement.

title: Directing an independent audit of the 2026 county budget
summary:
Commissioner Ivory's resolution would direct the County Manager to hire an independent outside contractor for a single-year comprehensive audit of the entire 2026 Fulton County budget, in a format similar to the Annual Comprehensive Financial Report. The audit would break down every line item over $1 million and review all departments' travel expenses. The County Manager would post the procurement by September 1, 2026, aim to pick a vendor by the end of 2026, and give the Board periodic updates.

Earlier: a motion to approve failed on March 4, 2026. Removed from the March 18, 2026 agenda at the request of Chairman Pitts. It had not come back for a vote as of the board’s October 21, 2026 meeting.
whyItMayMatter: The county's 2026 budget, which the resolution says exceeds $1 billion, would get a detailed independent review, including all departments' travel costs.

title: Urging the General Assembly not to eliminate property taxes for local governments
summary:
Commissioner Ivory's resolution would urge the Georgia General Assembly not to pass legislation eliminating property taxes as a source of local government revenue, and to consider the effect on counties' ability to provide services. It points to proposals including the HOME Act, HR 1114 and HB 1116, and says about 80% of the county's annual revenue comes from property taxes. Copies would go to Fulton's legislative delegation and state House and Senate leaders. It does not itself change state law.

Earlier: a motion to approve failed on March 4, 2026. Removed from the March 18, 2026 agenda at the request of Chairman Pitts. It had not come back for a vote as of the board’s October 21, 2026 meeting.
whyItMayMatter: The resolution says property taxes provide about 80% of county revenue, which funds services such as public safety, courts and public health.

title: Supporting south downtown small businesses, including in 2026 World Cup opportunities
summary:
Commissioner Barrett's resolution would approve using Fulton County's Westside Tax Allocation District money to help small businesses in South Downtown ahead of the 2026 World Cup. It would allow $50,000 total, $12,500 each, toward Invest Atlanta Small Business Improvement Grants for four businesses: Delilah's Everyday Soul, The Vick at Healey, Crates and Bottle Rocket Fine Food & Beverage. It would also allow $62,500 for the Downtown Pop-Up Opportunity Fund, which gives $5,000 to $50,000 grants to help local shops and restaurants open in storefronts.

Approved March 18, 2026, 6–0.
whyItMayMatter: Four women- and minority-owned businesses near Mercedes-Benz Stadium would receive the county's share of grants already awarded to them.

title: Affirming constitutional rights at county facilities and limiting ICE enforcement
summary:
Commissioner Arrington's resolution would bar county officials and employees from letting law enforcement doing enforcement work, including ICE and Customs and Border Protection, into non-public areas of county facilities without a warrant signed by a judge. It would direct the Fulton County Police Department to document federal immigration enforcement at county facilities and in unincorporated areas, record it on body cameras, report suspected violations of law, and give medical aid to anyone injured. The county would publish data on reported violations.

Earlier: held on February 18, 2026. Approved with changes on March 4, 2026, 5–0, with 1 abstaining and 1 not voting. The approved version differs from the original proposal; the item record has the details.
whyItMayMatter: Non-public areas of county buildings, such as employee work areas, would be off-limits to immigration enforcement officers who do not have a judge-signed warrant.

title: Establishing standing committees of the Board of Commissioners
summary:
Commissioner Ivory's resolution would create seven standing committees of four or five commissioners each to review proposed agenda items in their subject areas before they go to the full Board. They would cover justice and safety, registration and elections, the budget, health and human services, animal services, rules, and arts and libraries. Committee meetings would be open to the public, held at least monthly at the Fulton County Government Center, and allow up to 30 minutes of public comment.

The board voted 5–2 on March 4, 2026 to file this item, which closes it without approving it.
whyItMayMatter: Residents could attend monthly public committee meetings and comment on proposed county business before it reaches the full Board.

title: At least two percent of the budget for new hospitals in Atlanta and South Fulton
summary:
Commissioner Ivory's resolution would reallocate at least two percent of the fiscal year 2026 budget toward costs related to establishing new hospitals in Atlanta and South Fulton. It would also direct the County Manager or his designee to propose at least a two percent allocation for that purpose in future budgets. The resolution cites the closing of Atlanta Medical Center and areas of South Fulton without nearby emergency medical facilities.

The board voted 4–3 on March 4, 2026 to file this item, which closes it without approving it.
whyItMayMatter: A share of the county budget would be set aside for new hospital projects in Atlanta and South Fulton, where the resolution says some areas lack nearby emergency care.

title: Planning intake diversion screening at the Rice Street Jail
summary:
Commissioner Ivory's resolution would direct the County Manager, with the Department of Finance, to work with the Sheriff's Office, the District Attorney's Office and the Office of the Solicitor-General on a plan for staffing at the Rice Street Jail intake facility to review charges and send eligible people to diversion programs before booking is finished. The plan would cover procedures, staffing, legal issues, coordination and projected costs, and would be due by the Board's first regular meeting in June, with a budget by the second meeting in July.

Removed from the March 4, 2026 agenda at the request of Commissioner Ivory. It had not come back for a vote as of the board’s October 21, 2026 meeting.
whyItMayMatter: Under the plan, eligible people entering the Rice Street Jail could be redirected to diversion programs before booking is complete.

title: Funding for capital purposes at Zoo Atlanta through the Recreation Authority
summary:
Commissioner Ivory's resolution would pay $145,947.06 that the county received in November 2023 from a Zoo Atlanta repair fund to the Atlanta Fulton County Recreation Authority, to be held for capital purposes at Zoo Atlanta. The money was distributed after the zoo's Series 2007 bonds were paid off, and the zoo operator would request it for eligible improvements at the main zoo and the Cyclorama building. The county would also notify the City of Atlanta so the city can consider returning its share.

Held on March 4, 2026 by a 5–2 vote. It had not come back for a vote as of the board’s October 21, 2026 meeting.
whyItMayMatter: Zoo Atlanta's operator could request $145,947.06 in county-returned funds for capital improvements at the zoo.

summary:

It would direct the County Manager and Finance Department to propose a fiscal year 2027 budget with at least $4.8 million for the same purpose. Permanent supportive housing pairs affordable housing with voluntary services such as case management and mental health treatment.

The board voted 4–3 on February 4, 2026 to file this item, which closes it without approving it.

The committee would make recommendations on tax allocation bond proceeds, meet at least quarterly and report to the Board twice a year.

It is worth up to $12.08 million over five years, through December 31, 2030, with two one-year renewal options. The monitors are also used to bill other jurisdictions under wastewater agreements and to plan sewer capacity.

title: Reinstating the Budget Commission and redefining its membership
summary:
Commissioner Ivory's resolution would repeal a 2018 resolution (18-0577) that replaced the county Budget Commission with a process in which the County Manager alone prepares the proposed budget. It would bring back the Budget Commission and expand it to include the Board Chairman or a staff designee, the County Manager, top finance and operations officials, and one staff representative chosen by each other commissioner. The County Manager would present a policy on how the commission works within 60 days.

On January 21, 2026 the board voted 4–2, with 1 absent, to file this item, which closes it without approving it.
whyItMayMatter: Staff from every commissioner's office would take part in preparing the county's proposed annual budget.

title: Pension rule change letting retired officers work as detention officers beyond hour limit
summary:
Commissioners Barrett, Abdur-Rahman and Ivory's resolution would change county pension rules so retired Sheriff's Office detention officers and sworn officers who hold detention officer certification could work as detention officers through December 31, 2026 without penalty to their pension, no matter how many hours they work. It responds to a jail staffing shortage tied to a federal consent decree. It would also end the pay penalty for rehired retirees who work no more than 1,040 hours a year.

Approved January 21, 2026, 5–0, with 1 absent and 1 not voting.
whyItMayMatter: Certified retired officers could fill Fulton County Jail detention officer jobs in 2026 while still receiving their existing pension.

title: Amending policies limiting Commissioners' use of county staff for events
summary:
This resolution from Commissioners Ellis and Thorne would replace the 2024 policies (Resolution 24-0247) on when commissioners may use county staff for their events. Commissioners would rely mainly on their own district staff and budgets. They could request certain county staff for up to four town hall events a year, while other events, such as grand openings, ribbon cuttings and third-party events, would be handled by commissioners and their own staff.

Earlier: a motion to approve failed on December 17, 2025. Approved January 7, 2026, 4–3.
whyItMayMatter: The resolution says the goal is to keep county staff focused on their day-to-day work and avoid unnecessary overtime pay.

title: Affirming reproductive rights and urging repeal of the six-week abortion ban
summary:
Commissioner Barrett's resolution would affirm that reproductive rights are human rights and condemn the criminalization of reproductive care, abortion and related services. It would urge the Georgia General Assembly and the Governor of Georgia to repeal the state's six-week abortion ban (HB 481), and direct the Clerk to send copies to each member of the General Assembly. The resolution states the county's position; it would not itself change state law.

Earlier: a motion to approve failed on December 3, 2025; a motion to approve failed on December 17, 2025. The motion to approve failed on January 7, 2026 (3 yes, 3 no, 1 abstaining).

title: Establishing a Fulton County Women's Commission
summary:
Commissioner Barrett's resolution would create a Fulton County Women's Commission to advise the Board of Commissioners on strategies, policies, funding and partnerships to improve women's lives. It would address issues such as women's rights, access to health care and health outcomes, and economic security and gender equity in the workplace. Members would be appointed by the commissioners, and the County Manager would assign staff support. Within six months of convening, it would present its bylaws, goals and a two-year action plan.

Earlier: a motion to approve failed on December 3, 2025; a motion to approve failed on December 17, 2025. The motion to approve failed on January 7, 2026 (3 yes, 1 no, 2 abstaining, 1 not voting).

title: Creating a Healthy Women, Healthy Families grant program
summary:
Commissioner Barrett's resolution would create a "Healthy Women, Healthy Families" grant program giving $1 million a year in grants to organizations serving women who live in Fulton County. Groups working on issues such as reproductive and maternal health, women's cancers, mental health and gender-based violence prevention could apply for grants of $50,000 to $100,000. The County Manager would deliver an implementation plan by April 1, 2026, so awards could be made by the end of 2026.

Earlier: a motion to approve failed on December 3, 2025; a motion to approve failed on December 17, 2025. The motion to approve failed on January 7, 2026 (3 yes, 1 no, 2 abstaining, 1 not voting).
whyItMayMatter: Organizations serving women's health needs in Fulton County could apply for county grants of $50,000 to $100,000.

title: Urging the Georgia General Assembly to preserve the Board's role in local affairs
summary:
Commissioner Ivory's resolution would state the Board's support for its ability to govern local affairs. It would urge the Georgia General Assembly to preserve the Board of Commissioners' involvement in matters affecting Fulton County residents, and state the Board's opposition to any legislation that would eliminate or significantly restrict its discretion. Copies would go to the Fulton County legislative delegation and to Georgia House and Senate leadership.

Earlier: a motion to approve failed on December 3, 2025; a motion to approve failed on December 17, 2025. The motion to approve failed on January 7, 2026 (3 yes, 2 no, 1 abstaining, 1 not voting).

title: Revising the Veterans' Empowerment Commission's purpose and funding veterans programming
summary:
Commissioners Ellis and Abdur-Rahman's resolution would revise the purpose of the Fulton County Veterans' Empowerment Commission, an advisory body, so it works with county staff on veterans' services. It would dedicate $250,000 of Community Services Program funding to housing programs for veterans and $200,000 of Arts & Culture Contract for Services funding to veterans' arts programming. The commission would help with outreach on behavioral health, senior services and county jobs.

Approved January 7, 2026, 7–0.
whyItMayMatter: Veterans in Fulton County would have $250,000 for housing programs and $200,000 for arts programming set aside for them within existing county programs.

title: Free-standing emergency department contract with the Fulton DeKalb Hospital Authority
summary:
This resolution would approve a Free-Standing Emergency Department contract between the Fulton DeKalb Hospital Authority and Fulton County, along with related documents for the Authority's bond issuance. The contract concerns building, equipping and providing medical services and hospital facilities for the indigent sick in Fulton County. The county would pay what it owes under the contract from its General Fund, and would levy taxes under the Hospital Authorities Law only if general funds were not enough.

Approved December 17, 2025, 6–0, with 1 absent.
whyItMayMatter: County general funds would back a contract for emergency and hospital services for the indigent sick in Fulton County, with a tax levy allowed only if those funds fall short.

title: Urging state legislators to repeal the LIFE Act (House Bill 481)
summary:
Chairman Pitts's resolution would add to the county's 2026 legislative agenda a call urging Georgia House and Senate members to repeal House Bill 481, the LIFE Act, which bans abortions after a fetal heartbeat is detected, typically about six weeks into pregnancy. The Clerk would send a copy to each member of the General Assembly and to the Association County Commissioners of Georgia. The resolution states the county's position; it does not change state law.

Approved December 17, 2025, 4–1, with 2 absent.
whyItMayMatter: Fulton County's official 2026 legislative agenda would include asking state lawmakers to repeal HB 481.

title: Abolishing two clerk of court technology funds and moving their money to the General Fund

The money already in those funds, and future fees that would have gone into them, would be deposited into the County General Fund instead.

Removed from the December 17, 2025 agenda. It had not come back for a vote as of the board’s October 21, 2026 meeting.
whyItMayMatter: Court clerk technology fees would no longer be kept in dedicated funds and would go into the county's General Fund.

title: Creating a Commercial Property Assessment Task Force
summary:
Commissioner Ivory's resolution would create a Commercial Property Assessment Task Force to review how commercial properties are valued and advise the Board of Commissioners, working with the Fulton County Board of Tax Assessors. Each commissioner would appoint one unpaid member with real estate or appraisal expertise for a one-year term. The task force would not take over the Tax Assessors' legal authority, and it would end on December 31, 2026, unless the Board continued it.

Earlier: held on November 5, 2025; a motion to approve failed on November 19, 2025. The board voted 4–3 on December 3, 2025 to deny it.
whyItMayMatter: The resolution says it responds to public concern that commercial properties in Fulton County have been undervalued.

title: Rules for choosing a presiding officer when the Chairman and Vice-Chairman are absent
summary:
Commissioner Arrington's ordinance would change the county code's rules on who leads Board of Commissioners meetings when the Chairman is absent. The vice chair would preside; if the vice chair is also absent, the commissioner with the most seniority would preside, then the next most senior commissioner present. If two or more commissioners have equal seniority, the members present would choose among them by majority vote.

Earlier: a motion to approve failed on November 19, 2025. The board voted 4–3 on December 3, 2025 to deny it.
whyItMayMatter: The ordinance says unclear rules could cause uncertainty or delay in holding Board meetings when both the chair and vice-chair are absent.

title: Directing development of a Senior Property Tax Relief Program
summary:
Commissioner Ivory's resolution would direct the County Manager to work with the Chief Operating Officer, Select Fulton and the Fulton County Development Authority to design a program offering property tax relief and housing stability for senior residents. They would also identify or help create a non-profit fund to pay for it. A proposed framework, including eligibility and funding recommendations, would be due to the Board by the second regular meeting in February 2026.

Earlier: a motion to approve failed on November 19, 2025. The board voted 4–3 on December 3, 2025 to deny it.
whyItMayMatter: Senior homeowners facing higher property tax bills would be the intended beneficiaries of the proposed program.

summary:

whyItMayMatter: Medical and mental health care for people held in the Fulton County Jail would continue under this contract through 2026.

title: Funding program for non-profits serving people in contact with the justice system
summary:
Commissioner Ivory's resolution would create a program to fund non-profit and community groups that serve people who come into contact with the Fulton County justice system, including the courts, District Attorney, Solicitor General, Public Defender, Sheriff's Office and Police. These justice agencies would jointly review proposals and recommend awards, with the Board giving final approval. The County Manager and Director of Finance would set aside at least $3 million of the FY2026 Non-Agency budget for the program.

On December 3, 2025 the board voted 4–2, with 1 abstaining, to deny it.
whyItMayMatter: People dealing with Fulton County courts and law enforcement could get help from community organizations funded through the program.

title: Purchase of automated external defibrillators for the Fulton County Police Department
summary:
Chairman Pitts' resolution would approve buying automated external defibrillators (AEDs) for the Fulton County Police Department, at a total cost of up to $225,000 from opioid settlement funds. The AEDs would be placed in patrol vehicles and at police offices. The department would have to train staff expected to use them in CPR and AED use, and set a policy for storing, inspecting and maintaining the devices.

Approved December 3, 2025, 7–0.
whyItMayMatter: Police officers, who are often first to arrive at medical emergencies, would have AEDs to help people in sudden cardiac arrest.

title: Extending the Reparations Task Force for twelve months
summary:
Chairman Pitts' resolution would extend the Fulton County Reparations Task Force for 12 months past its current end date of December 31, 2025, keeping it in place through December 31, 2026. The task force was created in April 2021 to research the feasibility of slavery reparations for Black/African-Americans living in Fulton County. Current members would stay on, and the group would keep the same structure and duties.

Approved November 19, 2025, 4–0, with 1 abstaining and 1 absent and 1 not voting.
whyItMayMatter: The task force would get more time to do research and prepare recommendations for the Board of Commissioners.

title: Extending the Reparations Task Force for two years
summary:
Commissioner Arrington's resolution would extend the Fulton County Reparations Task Force for two years past its current end date of December 31, 2025, keeping it in place through December 31, 2027. The task force was created in April 2021 to research the feasibility of slavery reparations for Black/African-Americans living in Fulton County. Current members would stay on, and the group would keep the same structure and duties.

whyItMayMatter: The task force would get more time to do research and prepare recommendations for the Board of Commissioners.

title: Addressing maternal and infant mortality rates
summary:
Commissioners Ivory and Barrett's resolution would direct the County Manager to review the county's current capital investments and planned projects to see how they could be used to address maternal and infant mortality in Fulton County. The County Manager would develop a plan with strategies, timelines and coordination among county departments, and present it to the Board at a future public meeting.

Approved November 19, 2025, 6–0, with 1 absent.
whyItMayMatter: The plan would aim to support better health outcomes for mothers and infants in Fulton County.

title: Raising Boards of Equalization member pay from $100.00 to $150.00 per day
summary:
Commissioner Arrington's resolution would raise the pay for each member of the Fulton County Boards of Equalization from $100 per day to $150 per day. These boards hear and decide appeals of property tax assessments and denials of homestead exemptions. The resolution would also have the daily rate rise along with county-wide cost-of-living increases for Fulton County employees.

Earlier: held on October 1, 2025; a motion to approve failed on October 15, 2025. The motion to approve failed on November 5, 2025 (3 yes, 4 no).
whyItMayMatter: Members of the boards that hear residents' property tax assessment appeals would be paid $150 per day instead of $100.

summary:
Commissioner Ivory's resolution would direct the County Manager to include a review of animal services in each quarterly operational report to the Board of Commissioners, beginning January 1, 2026. The review would cover field control services, shelter operations, and enforcement.

whyItMayMatter: The Board would get regular reports on animal control and shelter operations, which the resolution says would help it identify issues and track progress over time.

title: Addressing food insecurity with more support for non-profit partners and senior nutrition
summary:
Chairman Pitts' resolution responds to the loss of SNAP food benefits during the federal shutdown. It would add $500,000 for nine non-profits the county already funds, $150,000 for senior nutrition (winter farmers markets, a free to-go meal for seniors on SNAP who buy a meal at county senior centers, and home-delivered meals), and $50,000 for the Fulton Fresh produce program. It would also direct Finance and Public Works not to shut off residential water for non-payment from November 5 through December 31, 2025.

Approved with changes on November 5, 2025, 7–0. The approved version differs from the original proposal; the item record has the details.
whyItMayMatter: Residential water customers would be protected from shutoffs for non-payment through December 31, 2025, and food aid would increase through county partners and senior programs.

title: Declaring a local State of Emergency over SNAP benefit suspension and food insecurity
summary:
Commissioners Barrett and Arrington's resolution would declare a local State of Emergency in Fulton County because federal SNAP food benefits were suspended during the government shutdown. It would authorize spending up to $4.4 million of an expected $69 million in 2025 budget underruns on the crisis, and direct the County Manager to find the most effective strategies and partner organizations. The emergency would last up to 60 days and could be renewed or suspended by the Board.

The motion to approve failed on November 5, 2025.
whyItMayMatter: Residents who lost SNAP food benefits would be the focus of up to $4.4 million in county food-aid spending.

title: Directing a Project Care public health plan to address healthcare disparities
summary:
Commissioner Barrett's resolution would direct County management to create a "Project Care" public health strategic plan to address health care gaps in Fulton County, building on a 2023 study called "Project Care." The plan would focus especially on South Fulton communities, which the study called a "healthcare desert." It would include key performance indicators, budget recommendations for the FY2026 budget, and quarterly reports to the Board of Commissioners.

The board voted 4–3 on October 1, 2025 to file this item, which closes it without approving it.
whyItMayMatter: Residents of South Fulton, where the study found people must travel long distances for emergency and primary care, would be a particular focus of the plan.

title: Administrative holidays in December 2025 and January 2026
summary:
Chairman Pitts's resolution would make Friday, December 26, 2025, and Friday, January 2, 2026, Administrative Holidays for Fulton County government. Because the December 24-25 and December 31-January 1 holidays both fall on Wednesday and Thursday, this would spare most employees from returning to work for just one day before the weekend. County offices, including the government centers and courthouse, would close on those Fridays, and essential employees who must work would earn holiday leave for each hour worked.

Approved September 17, 2025, 6–0, with 1 absent.
whyItMayMatter: Fulton County government offices, including the government centers and courthouse, would be closed on December 26, 2025 and January 2, 2026.

title: Urging release of Israeli hostages and a permanent ceasefire in Israel and Gaza
summary:
Commissioner Arrington's resolution expresses Fulton County's sorrow over the loss of Israeli civilians in the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack and the loss of innocent Palestinian lives in the war since. It urges Israel and Hamas to agree to an immediate and permanent ceasefire, urges Hamas to release all hostages, and urges Israel to lift all restrictions on humanitarian aid entering Gaza.

title: Ending the HIV Epidemic service contracts (federally funded)
summary:
These are federally funded "Ending the HIV Epidemic" service contracts between Fulton County and subrecipient organizations that deliver or enhance HIV-related care and support services in the 20-county Atlanta area. Yearly limits would range from about $5.19 million for the rest of FY2025 (starting August 1, 2025) to about $6.34 million in FY2029. The money comes from a Health Resources and Services Administration award and is 100% grant funded with no Fulton County match. The Chairman would be authorized to sign the contracts.

Approved August 6, 2025 as part of the consent agenda.
whyItMayMatter: Organizations providing HIV-related care and support services in the Atlanta area would receive federal funding through these county-managed contracts.

title: Requiring annual training assessments from department heads during budgeting
summary:
Commissioner Ivory's resolution would require each department head who seeks County money for training and related travel to complete an annual training assessment during budget preparation. The assessment would show the department's progress on the current year's training goals and its training and travel needs for the next year, and the Board would use it when reviewing the proposed budget. It would also direct the County Manager to update Personnel Procedure 209-16, the travel and training policy, within 60 days.

Earlier: held on June 18, 2025. Removed from the July 9, 2025 agenda at the request of Commissioner Ivory. It had not come back for a vote as of the board’s October 21, 2026 meeting.
whyItMayMatter: The Board would receive a yearly assessment of each department's training and travel needs when it reviews the county budget.

title: Contract renewal: Behavioral Health Crisis Center operation (Grady Health System)
summary:
This renews the county's contract with Grady Memorial Hospital, doing business as Grady Health System, to fully operate and manage the Fulton County Behavioral Health Crisis Center. The renewal would cost up to about $12.62 million and run through June 30, 2026. It is the second of eight renewal options under the Fulton County Behavioral Health Network contract, leaving six more.

Approved July 9, 2025, 7–0.
whyItMayMatter: Grady would continue running the county's Behavioral Health Crisis Center through June 30, 2026.

title: Speeding jail overtime and staffing incentive funds to the Sheriff for detention officers
summary:
Commissioner Barrett's resolution would speed up jail staffing money by moving funds the Board created in Resolution #25-0360 into the Sheriff's Office budget to help recruit and keep detention officers. It would transfer the $1 million staffing incentive fund and $3,592,984 in overtime funds for quarters 2 and 3 right away, and $1,796,492 for the 4th quarter on October 1, 2025 after verifying earlier funds were spent as intended. It would drop the requirement for a complete staff roster and attestation, and ask for copies of reports required by the Consent Decree.

The board voted 5–2 on July 9, 2025 to file this item, which closes it without approving it.
whyItMayMatter: The Sheriff's Office would get overtime and hiring-incentive money for jail detention staffing that the resolution says had been delayed more than two months.

title: Ending county participation and tax payments in the Westside Tax Allocation District
summary:
Commissioners Ellis and Abdur-Rahman's resolution would end Fulton County's participation in new projects in the Westside Tax Allocation District, created by the Atlanta City Council. The county would not consent to new projects, or to sending county tax increments to the City, after July 9, 2025, and the Tax Commissioner would stop sending them unless the Board later approves. The resolution says the county has paid nearly $96 million into the district, with a yearly increment of about $9.4 million, and wants that revenue used for services for all residents.

Held on July 9, 2025 by a 7–0 vote. It had not come back for a vote as of the board’s October 21, 2026 meeting.
whyItMayMatter: County tax money now going to the Westside Tax Allocation District would stay with the county, which the resolution says would help avoid unnecessary property tax rate increases.

title: Affirming county fringe benefits for Superior Court judges
summary:
Commissioner Ivory's resolution, co-sponsored by Commissioners Thorne and Ellis, lists in writing the County fringe benefits offered to Superior Court Judges of the Atlanta Judicial Circuit as of June 30, 2025. A new state law, House Bill 85, creates locality pay for these judges but lets counties keep providing benefits as they were on that date. The benefits include health, life, dental and vision insurance, 401(a) and 457(b) plans, disability insurance and retiree health coverage. They would continue for current judges, and could be offered to new judges, if funded each year.

Approved June 18, 2025, 7–0.
whyItMayMatter: Superior Court Judges of the Atlanta Judicial Circuit who opt into the new state locality pay would have a written list of the county benefits that remain available to them.

title: Agreement with Atlanta on tax foreclosure for city code enforcement liens
summary:
Chairman Pitts's resolution would approve an agreement among Fulton County, the Fulton County Tax Commissioner and the City of Atlanta for the Tax Commissioner to collect and enforce certain city code enforcement liens through the judicial in rem foreclosure process. Such liens can cover the city's costs to repair, close or demolish unsafe buildings. The city would pay the county an administration fee, outside attorneys hired by the county would be paid, and the Tax Commissioner would receive nothing.

whyItMayMatter: Owners of City of Atlanta properties with unpaid code enforcement liens could face judicial foreclosure on those liens through the Tax Commissioner.

title: Tax billing and collection agreement with Palmetto
summary:
Commissioner Arrington's resolution would approve an agreement for the Fulton County Tax Commissioner to bill and collect the City of Palmetto's municipal property (ad valorem) taxes each year. Palmetto now handles its own tax billing and collection. Under the agreement, the city would pay the county for the use of county staff and resources, the Tax Commissioner could receive compensation, and the term could be up to 50 years.

Approved May 7, 2025, 5–1, with 1 absent.
whyItMayMatter: Palmetto property owners would have their city property taxes billed and collected by the Fulton County Tax Commissioner.

title: Overtime pay and incentives to staff and retain jail detention officers and deputies
summary:
Vice Chair Ellis's resolution would set up two general fund accounts to help hire and keep detention officers and deputies who work full time in Fulton County jails: a Detention Services Overtime Fund with $1 million set aside quarterly for overtime, and a one-time $1 million Detention Services Staffing Incentive Fund. Both end by December 31, 2025, with quarterly reports. The Sheriff must give the board a staff roster each quarter to use the money, and the board urges the Sheriff to limit non-core services.

Approved with changes on May 7, 2025, 5–0, with 1 abstaining and 1 absent. The approved version differs from the original proposal; the item record has the details.
whyItMayMatter: The resolution cites 144 vacant Sheriff's Office positions as of March 25, 2025, mostly in detention roles, and directs this money only to jail detention staff.

title: Westside Tax Allocation District funding for three projects
summary:
Commissioner Barrett's resolution would approve using Fulton County property tax increment from the Westside Tax Allocation District for three grants approved by Invest Atlanta: up to $260,000 to turn a building at 471 English Avenue into six apartments; up to $3.5 million to stabilize, preserve and convert vacant property at 143 Alabama Street into apartments and retail space; and up to $400,000 for the Westside Future Fund to build or redevelop four single-family homes in English Avenue and Vine City.

Earlier: held on March 19, 2025; held on April 2, 2025. Approved April 16, 2025, 4–1, with 2 abstaining.
whyItMayMatter: The grants are meant to produce affordable housing, including 46 affordable units planned at 143 Alabama and four homes kept permanently affordable.

title: Replacing county rules on recognition of employee organizations
summary:
Chairman Pitts's resolution would repeal and replace county code sections 154-36 through 154-44 on employee organizations, to streamline how the board recognizes them and remove outdated names and processes. The current code requires a group to be chosen by 50 percent plus one of eligible employees, or have 300 or more eligible members, before meeting with county officials. The new text has a group file a written request with the County Manager, and the board may recognize it at its discretion.

Approved April 16, 2025, 6–0, with 1 not voting.
whyItMayMatter: Recognized employee organizations can meet and confer with the county on wages, hours and working conditions, and members can have dues deducted from their paychecks.

title: Pilot program to reimburse child care expenses
summary:
Chairman Pitts's resolution would let the County Manager run a pilot program from July 1 through December 31, 2025, reimbursing up to $500 per month per employee for child care. It would be open to benefits-eligible employees in county-funded positions, not state-funded ones, for child care centers within 1.5 miles of the Fulton County Government Center, such as Bright Horizons. It also authorizes a separate child care program near the Rice Street Jail to help keep and recruit jail officers.

Approved with changes on April 16, 2025, 7–0. The approved version differs from the original proposal; the item record has the details.
whyItMayMatter: Eligible county employees could be reimbursed up to $500 a month for child care in late 2025; a county survey found 166 employees would consider taking part.

title: Opening the senior Adult Day Health Program to county employees
summary:
Chairman Pitts's resolution would open the Department of Senior Services' Adult Day Health Program, now limited to Fulton County residents, to seniors cared for by employees in county-funded positions, wherever they live. They would follow the same rates, fees, application process, availability and rules as residents. The program offers meals, health monitoring and activities for seniors with physical or cognitive limitations. State employees in state-funded positions are not included.

Approved April 16, 2025, 6–0, with 1 absent.
whyItMayMatter: County employees who care for seniors and live outside Fulton County could enroll those seniors in the county's adult day program.

title: Appointment to the Fulton County Citizens Commission on the Environment
summary:
Approved March 19, 2025 as part of the consent agenda.

The agenda describes it as: “FULTON COUNTY CITIZENS COMMISSION ON THE ENVIRONMENT The Fulton County Citizens Commission on the Environment shall consist of citizens from throughout Fulton County to be appointed by the Members of the Board of Commissioners. There shall be fourteen (14) members to serve on the Commission. In making such appointments, the Fulton County Board of Commissioners shall ensure that the terms of appointment are staggered. Each District Commissioner shall appoint one Commission member to a four (4) year term. Each District Commissioner shall also appoint one Commission member to a two (2) year term to ensure staggered terms. After the expiration of each appointee’s initial term, the regular term of office for such an appointee shall be four (4) years. No term of any member shall extend beyond the term of the District Commissioner who appointed the member to serve on the Fulton County Citizens Commission on the Environment; however, each member may continue to serve beyond his/her term until replaced. After the expiration of any appointee’s initial term, the Commission may recommend to the Fulton County Board of Commissioners a list of eligible persons for consideration as appointees to the Commission. The Appointing member of the Fulton County Board of Commissioners may remove his/her appointee(s) to this Commission at any time and within the sole discretion of that individual of the Fulton County Board of Commissioners. Term below expired: 12/31/2024 Ron Comacho (District 3) Commissioner Barrett nominated Ron Comacho for a District reappointment to a term ending December 31, 2025.”

title: Accepting food, Naloxone and fentanyl test strip donations for the Deflection Team
summary:
This resolution by Chairman Pitts and Commissioners Ivory and Abdur-Rahman would accept ongoing food donations from Intown Collaborative Ministries, Inc. and the Atlanta Community Food Bank, and naloxone and fentanyl testing strips from Georgia Harm Reduction Coalition, Inc. The items would go to the county behavioral health department's Deflection Team, whose outreach aims to steer people with substance use issues from jail into treatment. The donations' value is undetermined.

Approved March 19, 2025, 7–0.
whyItMayMatter: People reached by the Deflection Team's outreach in North and South Fulton could receive food, naloxone and fentanyl testing strips.

title: Urging Georgia House members to vote no on Senate Bill 244 on criminal proceeding costs
summary:
Commissioner Barrett's resolution would urge members of the Georgia House of Representatives to vote no on Senate Bill 244. As the resolution describes it, SB 244 would let a criminal defendant recover attorney's fees and costs when a prosecutor is disqualified for misconduct, paid from the treasury of the county where the case was brought. It would also direct the Clerk to send copies to each House member and the Association County Commissioners of Georgia.

The board voted 5–2 on March 19, 2025 to file this item, which closes it without approving it.
whyItMayMatter: The resolution states the board's view that fee awards under SB 244 would be paid from Fulton County's treasury and affect county taxpayers; the resolution itself does not change state law.

title: Operation Public Servant: recruiting displaced federal employees
summary:
Chairman Pitts's resolution would create Operation Public Servant, under which Fulton County would offer a courtesy interview to people who lost federal jobs in 2025 because of Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) actions, or took early retirement offers, and who qualify for a vacant county position. The resolution notes the county has almost 800 vacant funded positions. It encourages, but does not require, other officials whose staff the county pays to do the same.

Approved March 19, 2025, 5–0, with 2 not voting.
whyItMayMatter: Qualified former federal workers displaced in 2025 who apply for county jobs would be guaranteed an interview.

title: Leasing Camp Truitt land to the City of College Park for a botanical garden
summary:
Chairman Pitts's resolution would approve a ground lease letting the City of College Park use part of Camp Truitt, county-owned land at 4300 Herschel Rd in College Park, to build a city botanical garden and nature facility with supporting buildings and parking. The lease would run 50 years with an optional 50-year extension. The city would have to show within 90 days that it has money to build and run the project, and any income from it would be limited to uses allowed by the property's deed.

Approved with changes on March 5, 2025, 7–0. The approved version differs from the original proposal; the item record has the details.
whyItMayMatter: The resolution says the project would give Fulton County residents more park space and opportunities for nature education.

title: Budget increase for the Arts and Culture Contracts for Services program
summary:
Commissioners Barrett and Arrington's resolution would amend the FY2025 budget to give the Department of Arts and Culture an extra $1.7 million for its Contracts for Services (CFS) Program, to keep services at the level of FY2024 and recent years. The money would come from cutting the county's Non-Agency budget line by the same amount. The CFS Program funds nonprofit and other groups that offer ongoing public arts programs for Fulton County residents.

Earlier: a motion to approve failed on February 5, 2025. Removed from the February 19, 2025 agenda at the request of Commissioner Barrett. It had not come back for a vote as of the board’s October 21, 2026 meeting.
whyItMayMatter: Arts groups funded through the county's Contracts for Services Program would see funding kept at the level of recent years.

summary:
This item would have Chairman Robert L. Pitts sign a TEFRA certificate, a federal tax-law approval step, for the Development Authority of Fulton County to issue up to $45 million in revenue bonds for Spelman College. The bonds would refinance Spelman's Series 2012 and Series 2015 bonds, which paid for buildings and improvements on its campus, and cover issuing costs. The bonds would be repaid by the college, and the approval creates no financial liability for Fulton County.

title: Funding to comply with the Consent Decree
summary:
Commissioner Arrington's resolution would commit more county money to Fulton's criminal justice offices to help meet a federal court Consent Decree on jail conditions entered January 6, 2025. It lists about $1.51 million for the Clerk of Superior Court, $2.61 million for the Solicitor General, $4.9 million for the Public Defender, $12.5 million for the District Attorney, and at least $77.5 million initially for the Sheriff, much of it for hiring and keeping staff.

Removed from the January 29, 2025 agenda at the request of Commissioner Arrington. It had not come back for a vote as of the board’s October 21, 2026 meeting.
whyItMayMatter: The resolution says the added funding would help the justice offices better care for people held at the Fulton County Jail and reduce the jail population.

summary:

The list includes clothing, mattresses, blankets, hygiene and cleaning supplies, toilet tissue, law library books, and Narcan nasal spray for officers. title: Ryan White Part A HIV service contract extensions and funding increase
summary:
This item would extend the county's existing Ryan White Part A HIV service contracts for three months, from March 1, 2025, through May 31, 2025. Subject to federal funding, it would also raise the spending limit for the provider groups (subrecipients) by about $5.65 million under a federal Health Resources and Services Administration award. The contracts are paid entirely by the grant, with no Fulton County match.

Approved January 8, 2025 as part of the consent agenda.
whyItMayMatter: People receiving HIV services through these county-funded providers would avoid an interruption in client services during the extension period.

title: Observing the 96th birthday of Reverend Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.
summary:
Commissioner Abdur-Rahman's resolution would have the Board of Commissioners join the national observance of the 96th birthday of the Reverend Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., who was born in Atlanta on January 15, 1929. It honors his life and legacy as Fulton County's greatest resident and urges all Fulton County citizens to take part in the observance. It also directs the Clerk to share the resolution throughout the county and with Dr. King's family.

Approved January 8, 2025, 7–0.
